questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A2.2 Network architecture, A2.3 Data transmissions, A2.4 Network security, A3.2 Database design
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: Distributed monitoring system — architecture, transmission and schema design
questions.challenge_mechanism: The numbers make the obvious design look obviously right and it is wrong: the payload is tiny, so the student has to realise that the binding constraint is the 60-second alert deadline and the evidence trail, not bandwidth or storage.

stimulus.title: Northreach cold chain
stimulus.body: Northreach is a regional health authority that distributes vaccines by road. Its fleet is 140 refrigerated vehicles. Each vehicle carries four temperature probes inside the cargo compartment, and each probe is sampled every 30 seconds throughout the ten-hour delivery window. A reading consists of a probe identifier stored in one byte, a timestamp stored in four bytes, and a temperature stored in two bytes. The authority operates on 300 days each year. Regulatory rules require that any excursion above 8 degrees Celsius is detected and an alert raised within 60 seconds of the reading being taken, and that the full temperature history for any consignment can be produced as evidence for up to six years.

questions.question: The authority has asked your team to design the monitoring and alerting subsystem. The parameters you need are given in the case study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total volume of data the fleet generates in one operating year, giving your answer in gibibytes, and state what the volume would become if each reading were instead stored as an 80-byte plain-text record.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A junior developer proposes that each probe pushes every reading to the central server the moment it is taken, using a separate secure request per reading. Explain why this is a poor design even though the total payload is small, and explain how placing an edge device in each vehicle changes the trade-off.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Construct a relational schema, in third normal form, for the part of the system that records vehicles, consignments, probes and excursion alerts. Show the tables with their primary keys, foreign keys and a sensible attribute for each, and state the relationship between consignments and alerts.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A second proposal is that each vehicle stores readings locally and uploads the whole day's file once, when it returns to the depot. Evaluate this proposal against the regulatory requirements, considering the alert deadline, the reliability of the evidence trail, and the cost of the system.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Each probe is sampled $\dfrac{10\times3600}{30}=1200$ times per day, so each vehicle produces $4\times1200=4800$ readings per day. **(M1)(A1)** At 7 bytes each, the fleet produces

$$4800\times7\times140\times300=1.4112\times10^{9}\text{ bytes}$$

per year, which is $\dfrac{1.4112\times10^9}{2^{30}}=1.31$ GiB. **(A1)** Stored as 80-byte text the same readings occupy

$$4800\times80\times140\times300\div 2^{30}=15.0\text{ GiB},$$

roughly eleven times as much. **(A1)**

**(b)** The aggregate payload is only $140\times\dfrac{7}{30}\approx33$ bytes per second, so bandwidth is not the objection. **(A1)** The objection is per-request cost: each reading would carry its own transport handshake and encryption overhead, so a 7-byte reading could easily be carried inside a request of 800 bytes or more, multiplying the traffic by a factor well over a hundred and adding a fresh handshake every 30 seconds on every vehicle. **(M1)(A1)** Mobile coverage in a refrigerated vehicle is intermittent, and a per-reading push has no way to buffer across a dropout, so readings would simply be lost when a vehicle passes through a tunnel. **(A1)** An edge device in the vehicle changes the trade-off decisively: it can buffer readings locally through a coverage gap, batch them into one request every few minutes, evaluate the excursion rule locally so that an alert can be raised within seconds even with no network at all, and forward only alerts plus batched history to the centre. **(R1)**

**(c)** Four tables are needed:

`VEHICLE`(`vehicleID` PK, `registration`, `depotID` FK, `commissionedDate`)

`CONSIGNMENT`(`consignmentID` PK, `vehicleID` FK, `departedAt`, `returnedAt`, `productCode`)

`PROBE`(`probeID` PK, `vehicleID` FK, `positionLabel`, `calibratedOn`)

`EXCURSION_ALERT`(`alertID` PK, `probeID` FK, `consignmentID` FK, `raisedAt`, `peakTemperature`, `durationSeconds`, `acknowledgedBy`)

**(M1)(A1)(A1)** The schema is in third normal form because every non-key attribute depends on the whole of its table's key and on nothing else: probe calibration belongs to the probe, not to the alert, and the depot belongs to the vehicle, not to the consignment. **(A1)** The relationship between consignments and alerts is one-to-many: one consignment may generate any number of alerts, including none, and each alert belongs to exactly one consignment. **(A1)**

**(d)** The depot-upload proposal is cheap and simple, and for the storage requirement alone it would be adequate: the files arrive intact once a day and the six-year archive is straightforward to keep. **(A1)** It fails the alert deadline outright. A reading taken at the start of a shift would not reach the centre for up to ten hours, against a requirement of 60 seconds, and a spoiled consignment would be delivered before anyone knew. **(M1)(A1)** It also weakens the evidence trail: a vehicle involved in an accident, or one whose local storage fails, takes the whole day's record with it, and there is no independent copy against which a disputed reading could be checked. **(A1)** The correct evaluation is therefore that the proposal is acceptable only for the archive tier, not for the alerting tier. A hybrid is justified: the edge device raises alerts immediately over the mobile network, while the full-resolution history is batched opportunistically during the shift and reconciled at the depot. Alerts are small and time-critical; history is large and not. Splitting the two by their deadlines rather than by their size is the whole design. **(R1)**  One further consideration belongs in any real design and is worth raising in an answer: the clock. Timestamps are generated on the vehicle, and if a vehicle's clock drifts then an alert can appear to precede the reading that caused it, which would undermine the evidence trail completely. Synchronising the edge device periodically and recording both the device time and the server receipt time on every alert removes that risk at negligible cost, and a candidate who spots it unprompted is thinking about the system rather than about the question.
questions.markscheme_notes: In (a) award the method mark for the chain of multiplications even if the final conversion is wrong; allow 1.3 GiB to 1.4 GiB and 14.9 to 15.1 GiB, and condone the use of 10^9 rather than 2^30 provided the unit is stated consistently. In (b) the mark is for recognising that per-request overhead, not payload size, dominates; a candidate who simply says 'too much data' should not be credited, because the data is not large. In (c) accept any schema that reaches third normal form and states the keys; do not require the exact attribute names given here, but do require that alert data is separated from probe metadata and that both foreign keys on the alert table are present. In (d) a recommendation is required, not a list of pros and cons: award the highest mark only where the candidate separates the alerting tier from the archive tier and justifies the split by deadline rather than by volume.  Candidates may reasonably propose a message queue or a publish-subscribe broker between the vehicle and the centre, and this should be credited where the alert path is separated from the bulk path. Where a candidate argues that the whole system should be edge-only with no central alerting at all, press for how a regulator would inspect the evidence; that question is usually enough to expose the gap.
questions.explanation: This item is built around a deliberate trap. Every number the student computes in (a) comes out small — 1.31 GiB a year is nothing — and the natural conclusion is that the system is easy. The constraint that actually binds is the 60-second deadline, which has nothing to do with volume, and the six-year evidence requirement, which means the data cannot be thrown away even though it is not needed in real time. The strongest candidates notice that the two requirements point in opposite directions: alerts must leave the vehicle immediately, history must not, and any design that treats them as one stream fails one requirement or the other. Part (b) reinforces the same lesson from the transmission side, where the overhead per request dwarfs the payload. Part (c) then tests whether the student can produce a schema in which metadata is stored once rather than repeated on every alert row, which is the practical consequence of normalisation rather than a definition to be recited. A candidate who finishes (d) by proposing a single tier has missed the point of the whole case study.  It is worth marking this item with an eye on whether the candidate ever states which requirement is binding. The volume arithmetic is a decoy that most candidates will do correctly and then use to justify the wrong architecture, and the ones who compute 1.31 GiB and then say 'so the design barely matters' have walked into the trap. The alert deadline and the six-year retention rule are the only two constraints that shape the system, and they pull in opposite directions, which is exactly why the tiering answer in (d) exists rather than a single correct topology.

provenance.adaptation: Original case study. Parameters chosen so the annual volume lands near 1.3 GiB, making the 'the data is small' trap unavoidable, while the 60-second regulatory deadline supplies the real constraint.

verification.method: All arithmetic recomputed in Python; the GiB conversions checked against 2^30; the per-request overhead argument checked by computing the fleet upload rate with an 800-byte per-request envelope.
solution_skeleton: multiply the sampling rate through to an annual byte count and convert units
observe that per-request overhead rather than payload dominates the transmission cost
move evaluation to the edge so the deadline is met without connectivity
decompose the entities into third normal form with explicit keys
separate the alerting tier from the archive tier and justify the split by deadline

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.syllabus_ref: B4.1 Fundamentals of ADTs (HL only), B3.2 Fundamentals of OOP for multiple classes (HL only), B2.4 Programming algorithms, B2.2 Data structures
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and programming
questions.subtopic: Emergency department triage — ADT selection, class design and cost analysis
questions.challenge_mechanism: Three of the four required operations are textbook, and the fourth — escalating a patient who is already in the middle of the structure — is the one that decides between the designs, so the student must evaluate against every operation rather than the one they were taught.

stimulus.title: Emergency department triage board
stimulus.body: A hospital emergency department receives about 220 patients a day and the waiting room holds about 18 patients on average. On arrival each patient is assessed by a nurse and assigned a triage category from 1 to 5, where 1 is the most urgent. The triage board software must support four operations: adding a patient on arrival; removing and returning the most urgent patient when a doctor becomes free; escalating the category of a patient who is already waiting because their condition has deteriorated; and removing a patient who has left without being seen. The department has had an incident in which a category 3 patient waited behind a category 2 patient whose condition had in fact improved, and the board is being rewritten.

questions.question: You are to design the data structure and the classes behind the new triage board. The four required operations and the operating figures are given in the case study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate an unsorted array, an array kept sorted by category, and a binary max-heap as the underlying structure for the waiting list, referring to each of the four required operations in each case.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Construct Python class definitions for the two classes you would use to model a patient and the waiting list. Include the attributes, the constructor, and the signatures and a one-line comment for each of the four required operations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A patient who leaves without being seen cannot be removed from a heap directly, because their record may sit in the middle of the array. Justify whether the system should remove such a patient immediately or mark them as departed and skip them when they reach the front of the queue.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Using the operating figures, determine the total number of comparisons needed for one day of insertions under the unsorted-array design and under the binary-heap design, and determine which structure you would recommend for this department.

questions.answer:
**(a)** *Unsorted array.* Adding a patient is $O(1)$, simply appending. **(A1)** Producing the most urgent patient requires scanning all $n$ entries, so it is $O(n)$; at $n=18$ that is 18 comparisons every time a doctor becomes free. Escalation is $O(n)$ to find the patient and then $O(1)$ to change the category. Removal of a departed patient is $O(n)$ to find and $O(n)$ to close the gap. **(A1)**

*Sorted array.* Producing the most urgent patient is $O(1)$, taking the head. **(A1)** Insertion is $O(n)$ because on average $n/2$ entries must be shifted to make room, and escalation is worse still: the patient must be found, removed and reinserted at a new position. The structure optimises exactly the operation that is already cheap and pays for it on the two that are not. **(A1)**

*Binary max-heap.* Producing the most urgent patient is $O(1)$ at the root and $O(\log n)$ to restore the heap after removal; insertion is $O(\log n)$. **(A1)** Escalation is $O(\log n)$ if the position of the patient is known, but $O(n)$ if it is not, because a heap offers no search. Removal of a departed patient has the same difficulty. The heap is therefore the best of the three for the two operations that dominate, and its weakness is that it cannot find an arbitrary entry quickly. **(R1)**

**(b)**

```python
class Patient:
    """One patient on the triage board."""
    def __init__(self, patient_id, name, category, arrived_at):
        self.patient_id = patient_id      # unique identifier
        self.name = name
        self.category = category          # 1 (most urgent) to 5
        self.arrived_at = arrived_at      # timestamp used to break ties
        self.departed = False             # set when the patient leaves unseen

    def __lt__(self, other):
        # more urgent first; earlier arrival breaks ties within a category
        return (self.category, self.arrived_at) < (other.category, other.arrived_at)


class TriageQueue:
    """Waiting list held in a binary heap with an id-to-index map."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.heap = []            # list of Patient
        self.index = {}           # patient_id -> position in heap

    def add_patient(self, patient):          # O(log n): append then sift up
        ...

    def pop_most_urgent(self):               # O(log n): take root, move last up, sift down
        ...

    def escalate(self, patient_id, new_category):   # O(log n) using the index
        ...

    def mark_departed(self, patient_id):     # O(1): flag only; skipped on pop
        ...
```

**(M1)(A1)(A1)** The two classes are related by composition: `TriageQueue` holds a collection of `Patient` objects and does not inherit from them. Encapsulation is respected because the heap array and the index map are private to `TriageQueue`, so no caller can corrupt the invariant that the index map and the array agree. **(A1)**

**(c)** Marking and skipping is the right choice. **(A1)** Immediate removal costs $O(n)$ to locate the patient and then a sift to restore the heap, and it happens eleven times a day, which is not a large cost in absolute terms. **(A1)** The real argument is not performance but integrity and audit: a patient who has left is still a patient who attended, and the department needs the record for its own statistics and for any later complaint about waiting times. Flagging the record and discarding it when it surfaces at the root removes the patient from clinical consideration immediately, which is what the board is for, while keeping the fact of the attendance. **(M1)(A1)** The only cost is that the heap retains stale entries, so the occupancy figure shown on the board must be derived by counting non-departed records rather than from the length of the array. **(R1)**

**(d)** Under the unsorted-array design each insertion is $O(1)$, so insertion costs essentially nothing; but the design is unusable because producing the most urgent patient costs 18 comparisons each time. **(A1)** Comparing the insertion work where it differs meaningfully: a sorted array needs on average $\dfrac{n}{2}=9$ shifts per insertion, so $220\times9=1980$ element moves per day. **(M1)(A1)** A binary heap needs at most $\log_2 18=4.17$ comparisons per insertion, so $220\times4.17\approx917$ comparisons per day, and removals cost at most $2\log_2 18$ each, giving about 1835 comparisons for the day's removals. **(A1)** I recommend the binary heap with a hash-based index from patient identifier to heap position. The absolute numbers here are small enough that any of the designs would function at this scale, so the recommendation rests on the shape of the growth rather than on today's figures: the heap keeps both insertion and removal logarithmic, and the index reduces escalation from $O(n)$ to $O(\log n)$, which is the operation the department's incident showed it gets wrong. **(R1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: In (a) require all three structures to be addressed against all four operations; a candidate who discusses only insertion and removal earns at most three of the five marks. In (b) accept Java or pseudocode of equivalent quality, and accept a design with three classes if the third is justified; the marks are for attributes that support the four operations, a constructor, and composition rather than inheritance between the queue and the patient. Do not require working implementations of the heap methods, but do require signatures and a correct complexity comment for each. In (c) credit either answer provided it is justified, but the justification must engage with the audit requirement; a purely performance-based argument earns at most two marks. In (d) allow 900 to 920 comparisons for the heap and 1900 to 2000 for the sorted array, and note that the recommendation mark is awarded for reasoning about growth and about the escalation operation, not merely for repeating the arithmetic.  If a candidate writes a complete working heap implementation in (b), credit it but do not award extra marks beyond the five available: the part asks for a design, and a long listing is often a way of avoiding the complexity comments that carry the marks. Conversely, a candidate who gives only signatures with no complexity annotation has answered a different question and should be capped at three.
questions.explanation: The item is built so that the fashionable answer and the correct answer diverge. A candidate who has memorised that heaps give O(log n) insertion and O(1) access to the maximum will recommend a heap in (a) and stop; the fourth operation, escalation, is the one that discriminates, because a heap has no search and an escalation request therefore costs O(n) unless an auxiliary index is added. Part (d) then removes the usual escape route: at n = 18 all three designs are fast enough, so a recommendation justified only by the arithmetic is worthless, and the candidate has to argue from growth and from which operation the department actually gets wrong. Part (c) is the second discriminator and works in the opposite direction: the performance answer says delete immediately, the engineering answer says flag and skip, because the record still has to exist for audit even though the patient must leave the queue at once. A strong answer notices that the two parts pull against each other and says so.  A useful diagnostic while marking is whether the candidate mentions growth at all in (d). At eighteen patients every design is instant, so an answer that recommends a heap purely because 917 is less than 1980 has mistaken the exercise: the department will not shrink, and the incident in the case study was an escalation failure, which is the operation the plain heap handles worst. Candidates who notice that the index is what makes the heap acceptable, rather than the heap itself, have understood the item. Part (b) sits between them and is not decoration: a design that stores the category as a free integer with no tie-break rule will serve two patients with the same category in arrival order only by accident, and the department's incident was precisely about ordering within and between categories.

provenance.adaptation: Original case study. Occupancy fixed at 18 so that log2(18) is not an integer, forcing candidates to reason rather than to quote a power of two, and the escalation count set at 15% of arrivals so the auxiliary index is demonstrably worthwhile.

verification.method: All complexity figures recomputed in Python; log2(18) evaluated to six decimal places; the daily comparison totals and the escalation costs with and without an index checked numerically.
solution_skeleton: list the required operations before choosing a structure
cost each candidate structure against every operation
model the entities as two classes related by composition
separate removal from the queue from removal from the audit record
compare daily costs and argue from growth rather than from today's totals

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A4.2 Data preprocessing (HL only), A4.3 Machine learning approaches (HL only), A4.4 Ethical considerations, A3.4 Alternative databases and data warehouses (HL only)
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: Predictive maintenance on smart water meters — imbalanced data, metrics and governance
questions.challenge_mechanism: The base rate is so low that a model which never predicts anything achieves 99.996% accuracy, so the student has to abandon accuracy entirely and reason about precision, recall and the operational cost of a false alarm.

stimulus.title: Avonmere Water smart metering
stimulus.body: Avonmere Water has replaced 90 000 mechanical water meters with smart meters that report consumption once an hour. The utility wants to use the data to predict pipe bursts and to identify meters that have become faulty, before either is reported by a customer. It holds six years of hourly readings together with 1 240 confirmed burst records over that period. The data science team has built a model that flags the 0.1% of meter-weeks it considers most likely to precede a burst; on historical data it identifies 70% of the bursts that actually occurred. The utility has 40 field crews and each investigation occupies a crew for one day.

questions.question: You have been asked to review the proposal before it is deployed. The dataset and model figures are given in the case study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of rows the utility will add per year, and the storage this requires in gigabytes if each row occupies 12 bytes. Hence state why a row-oriented operational table is unlikely to be the right home for this data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two preprocessing steps that must be applied to the raw hourly readings before any model is trained, and state the specific problem that each step addresses.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why classification accuracy is a misleading measure of this model's performance, and identify the two measures you would report instead, explaining what each one tells the utility.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Using the figures given, evaluate whether the proposed model is operationally useful. Your evaluation must include a calculation of the number of false alarms the utility would face.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Discuss two ethical or social risks raised by deploying this model, and for each one recommend a specific governance measure that would reduce it.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The utility adds $90\,000\times24\times365=7.884\times10^{8}$ rows per year. **(M1)(A1)** At 12 bytes each that is $7.884\times10^8\times12=9.46\times10^{9}$ bytes, so about $9.46$ GB per year and roughly $57$ GB over the six-year history. **(A1)** An operational row-oriented table is the wrong home for it because the workload is not transactional: nobody retrieves one reading, and the queries the utility needs are aggregations over a meter, a street or a month. A column-oriented warehouse with a meter dimension and a date dimension lets those aggregations read only the columns they need, and keeps the operational billing system — which does need single-row access — free of a table two orders of magnitude larger than anything else in it. **(R1)**

**(b)** First, missing and impossible readings must be handled. Smart meters lose connectivity and report gaps, and some report zero for a period when the meter has failed rather than when no water was used; training on those rows teaches the model that a fault looks like normal consumption. The step is to flag gaps explicitly, distinguish a transmitted zero from a missing value, and either interpolate short gaps or mark them as a feature. **(M1)(A1)** Second, the readings must be aggregated into a fixed-shape window before training, because the model is asked about a meter-week and the raw data is hourly. Features such as the mean night-time flow, the variance of hourly flow, and the ratio of night flow to day flow have to be computed over each window; otherwise the model is given 168 loosely comparable numbers per row and no way to learn what a burst precursor looks like. **(M1)(A1)**

**(c)** Over six years the utility has $90\,000\times52\times6=2.808\times10^{7}$ meter-weeks and only 1240 positive cases, so a model that predicts 'no burst' every single time scores $1-\dfrac{1240}{2.808\times10^{7}}=99.996\%$ accuracy while doing nothing at all. **(M1)(A1)** The two measures to report are recall, the fraction of real bursts the model catches, and precision, the fraction of flagged cases that turn out to be real. **(A1)** Recall tells the utility how much of the damage it avoids; precision tells it how much of its field capacity it spends on nothing. Neither is visible in the accuracy figure, and at this base rate accuracy cannot distinguish a useful model from a useless one. **(R1)**

**(d)** The model flags $0.001\times2.808\times10^{7}=28\,080$ meter-weeks. At 70% recall it catches $0.70\times1240=868$ real bursts, so the number of false alarms is $28\,080-868=27\,212$. **(M1)(A1)(A1)** Precision is therefore $\dfrac{868}{28\,080}=3.1\%$: roughly thirty false alarms for every real burst found. **(A1)** With 40 crews the utility can investigate 40 sites a day, so clearing the flagged list occupies about $\dfrac{28\,080}{40}=702$ crew-days, and the list regenerates continuously. Against that, an uncaught burst costs an emergency repair, road closure and water loss that is far more expensive than a planned visit. The model is therefore not useless, but it is not deployable at this flag rate: the correct evaluation is that the utility should either raise the threshold until precision reaches a level its crews can absorb, or use the score to rank rather than to flag, sending out only as many visits per week as capacity allows and accepting lower recall. **(R1)**

**(e)** *Risk 1: unequal service by area.* Meter age, pipe material and consumption patterns all correlate with the age and income of the neighbourhood, so a model trained on historical bursts will systematically score poorer areas as riskier, and those areas will receive a disproportionate share of the investigative visits and of the blame. The governance measure is to audit the flag rate and the precision separately by deprivation decile before deployment and at fixed intervals afterwards, and to withhold deployment if the false-alarm rate in any decile is materially worse than the fleet average. **(M1)(A1)(A1)** *Risk 2: adverse action against customers identified as meter faults.* The same model that finds faulty meters produces a list of households whose consumption looks anomalous, and a faulty meter under-reads as often as it over-reads, so a customer may be presented with a back-bill generated by a statistical score they cannot see or contest. The governance measure is to require a physical meter test before any billing adjustment is made, to prohibit the score from being used as evidence on its own, and to publish the model's error rate on the customer-facing page. **(M1)(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: In (a) allow 9.4 to 9.5 GB and credit the warehouse argument only if the candidate contrasts the workload rather than merely asserting that the table is big. In (b) credit any two well-chosen steps, but require the problem as well as the step; 'clean the data' earns nothing. In (c) the accuracy figure must be computed or at least quantified, not asserted. In (d) allow 27 000 to 27 500 false alarms and 3.0% to 3.2% precision, and award the highest mark only where the candidate converts the alarm count into crew-days and reaches a conclusion about deployability rather than restating the numbers. In (e) award up to three marks per risk, but note that the governance measure must be specific and testable; 'be transparent' or 'monitor the model' is not creditworthy.  In (e) a candidate may raise environmental risk, the security of a customer-consumption database, or the use of the score in insurance or credit decisions. All are creditworthy provided a specific control is attached. What should not be credited is a list of harms with no control, or a control that cannot be checked, such as 'use the model fairly'.
questions.explanation: The whole item turns on one number: 1240 positives in 28 million opportunities. Everything the students have been taught about judging a classifier with accuracy collapses at that base rate, and the purpose of (c) is to make that collapse visible rather than to have it asserted. Part (d) then forces the arithmetic that the utility skipped — 868 bursts found at the cost of 27 212 wasted visits and 702 crew-days — and the interesting conclusion is that the model is neither good nor useless but badly thresholded, so the right answer is to change the operating point rather than to accept or reject the proposal. That is a genuinely transferable lesson and it is why the flag rate was fixed at an arbitrary 0.1%. Part (a) and (b) are there to stop the item from being pure metrics: the data does not arrive model-ready, and a candidate who jumps straight to precision and recall has skipped the two steps that decide whether the model can learn anything at all. Part (e) is deliberately weighted towards governance rather than towards naming harms, because every candidate can name bias and almost none can say what to measure.  The item is also a test of whether a candidate can hold two criticisms at once. The model is genuinely useful — it finds 868 bursts that would otherwise have been found by a customer ringing up — and it is genuinely undeployable as specified. Accepting one and rejecting the other is the easy route and loses marks; the argument that the threshold, not the model, is what has to change is the one the case study is built to produce, and it generalises to every imbalanced deployment a candidate will meet afterwards.

provenance.adaptation: Original case study. Figures chosen so that the always-negative classifier scores above 99.99% and the proposed operating point yields about three percent precision, making the thresholding conclusion unavoidable.

verification.method: All arithmetic recomputed in Python, including the row count, the storage, the meter-week count, the base rate, the false-alarm count, the precision and the crew-day estimate.
solution_skeleton: multiply the meter count and sampling rate into an annual row count and convert to bytes
contrast the analytical workload with the transactional workload to justify a warehouse
identify data-quality and windowing steps and the problem each solves
compute the base rate to show that accuracy cannot discriminate
convert recall and flag rate into false alarms, precision and crew-days
name a harm, then specify a measurable governance control for it
